title: coyomap
goal:
coyomap maps a codebase its owner no longer holds in their head. A coding agent can write more code than anyone follows. The code runs fine until the day somebody needs to understand it.

coyomap reads the project and writes a map. The map says what the product does, who it is for, and what it is made of. Every box on it carries a plain sentence and a link into the code.

A person browses the map in a drillable viewer, and opens code only where they need it. The map is stored beside the code and pinned to one commit. A later change can be measured against that pin.

roles.name: Map owner
roles.wants: a trustworthy map of their own project, and a cheap way to keep it in step with the code
roles.drives: UC1, UC2, UC3, UC4, UC7, UC8, UC9

roles.name: Map reader
roles.wants: to understand what a system does, top down, without reading all of its code

roles.name: Method author
roles.wants: to know whether a change to the instructions made the maps better or worse

glossary.meaning: The whole picture coyomap produces for one project: the diagrams, the plain sentence on every box, and the code links.
The map as currently accepted, pinned to one commit. A later code change is measured against it.
Analysing a project from scratch and writing a new map. It throws away hand edits to the old one.
The browser page that shows a map. It is served live and never stored as a file.
One tab in the viewer. Each answers a single question about the project.
One thing drawn on a view. An arrow between two boxes is a relation.
The file and line a box points at. A box without one is ungrounded, which counts as a defect.
One goal one party has, with the thing that starts it and the result it ends in.
A group of use cases that serve one goal of the product.
One end to end run through the use cases that tells the product's story, with nothing going wrong.
The numbered steps of one use case. Each step says who or what acts, on what.
A run of steps that several flows all run. It is written once and referred to by each of them.
One place the product meets something that is not the product.
One address, command or tool an interface is made of.
One crossing between a person and the product, at an interface, inside one flow.
One module sized piece of the code, drawn as a single box.
A group of components, and of smaller subsystems under it.
One real named type the code defines, with its fields and its links to other types.
One decision the product makes, written in product words, plus every place it is enforced.
The report saying what a code change does to the map.
Folding a change impact report into the baseline and re-pinning it.
The instructions a coding agent follows to build a map. Most of this product's real logic lives there, not in code.
The small file that lets a coding agent find this project and start following the instructions.
One worker's structured rows, written to a file and later merged into the map.
An automatic check a map must pass. Failing one is a defect in the map.
A check that reports rather than blocks. It is answered by a fix or by a recorded reason.
One statement the map makes about the code, which a fresh reader can try to disprove.
A fresh reader given a batch of claims and the code, told to disprove each one.
One skeptic's answer on one claim: it held up, the code contradicts it, or the code cannot settle it.
The count of how many claims were challenged and how they came out, stored in the map.
A measurement of the code tree, taken before the map is drawn. It says how heavy each folder is and where each name is defined.
Scoring two maps of one project to say whether a change to the instructions helped or hurt.
Reading a finished build and its chat to find what went wrong in the run.
The situation this product exists for. Your agent wrote a lot of code, it runs, and you no longer know what is under your feet.

stakes.stake: checks the map against newer code, accepts the result, and asks for edits by hand

capabilities.purpose: Puts the map in front of a person, drillable, with the code one click away.

stakes.stake: runs the local server that serves every map they own

use_cases.name: Install coyomap into a coding agent
use_cases.trigger: Someone who has cloned this project asks to install it.
use_cases.outcome: Their coding agent gains a new command, and the tools it drives are built and ready.

use_cases.name: Build a project's first map
use_cases.trigger: A person asks their coding agent for a map of a project that has none.
use_cases.outcome: A map of that project exists, pinned to the commit it describes.

use_cases.name: Leave code off the map
use_cases.trigger: A person names committed code the map is not meant to describe.
use_cases.outcome: Later maps leave that code out, and every count the tools print says so.

use_cases.name: Serve the maps on this machine
use_cases.trigger: A person starts the local map server.
use_cases.outcome: Every project they have mapped is listed on one page in their browser.

use_cases.name: Explore a project's map
use_cases.trigger: A person opens a project's map.
use_cases.outcome: They see what the product does and drill from one feature down to a single box.

use_cases.name: Open the code behind a box
use_cases.trigger: A reader picks the code link on a box.
use_cases.outcome: The file opens beside the map at that line. One more press hands it to their editor or the code host.

use_cases.name: See what a code change did to the map
use_cases.trigger: The code has moved on since the map was pinned.
use_cases.outcome: A report names the parts of the map the change touched.

use_cases.name: Fold a change report into the baseline
use_cases.trigger: A person agrees the change report is right.
use_cases.outcome: The map is edited to match, re-pinned, and checked again.

use_cases.name: Change the map by asking
use_cases.trigger: A person asks in plain language for a part of the map to move, split or be renamed.
use_cases.outcome: The map is edited in place and passes its checks.

use_cases.name: Score whether the method got better
use_cases.trigger: Someone changed the instructions and wants to know the cost.
use_cases.outcome: Two maps of one project are scored and compared, with a verdict.

use_cases.name: Review a finished build
use_cases.trigger: A build has finished and its chat is on disk.
use_cases.outcome: A report names the friction, the bugs and the gaps that run revealed.

happy_path.why: needs the command installed at HP1
needs a built map to serve, from HP2
needs the server running from HP3
needs a box on screen, reached at HP4
needs the pinned baseline written at HP2
needs the change report produced at HP6

subsystems.name: Method
subsystems.purpose: Holds the instructions a coding agent follows to build, check and ship a map. Most of this product's logic lives here, not in code.

subsystems.name: Map content instructions
subsystems.purpose: Says what a map must contain, one section at a time. It runs from the product story down to the code.

subsystems.name: Build process instructions
subsystems.purpose: Says how a build runs. Which mode to enter, how to split the work, how to verify it, how to close.

subsystems.name: Specs and worker briefs
subsystems.purpose: The stored shape of a map, the briefs handed to fan-out workers, and the checks that keep the instructions honest.

subsystems.name: Delivery and documentation
subsystems.purpose: How a coding agent finds this product, and what a person reads before using or changing it.

subsystems.name: Map data and checks
subsystems.purpose: Defines what a map is and merges each worker's rows into one. Refuses a map that is not well formed.

subsystems.name: Map data
subsystems.purpose: The typed shape of a map, its shared words, and the merge that turns many workers' rows into one map.

subsystems.name: Map checks
subsystems.purpose: Five families of check that ask whether a map is well formed, from its shape to its stored data.

subsystems.name: Build and upkeep commands
subsystems.purpose: The commands a coding agent runs during a build. Sizing, grouping, challenging the claims, closing, and measuring a later code change.

subsystems.name: Command surface
subsystems.purpose: What a person types, and what the briefing says before any work starts. Also what the run records about itself.

subsystems.name: Build steps
subsystems.purpose: Sizing the code and leaving parts of it out. Assigning every element to its group, and measuring how crowded each screen is.

subsystems.name: Verification and close
subsystems.purpose: Turns the map against itself and records how its claims held up. Applies the fixes, then runs the closing sequence.

subsystems.name: Map viewer
subsystems.purpose: Turns a stored map into pictures and serves them beside the project's own code. Draws the page a person reads.

subsystems.name: View data
subsystems.purpose: Builds every diagram and every page's facts from the stored map, on demand.

subsystems.name: Map server
subsystems.purpose: Serves the viewer page, the map data and the project's own files, on this machine only.

subsystems.name: Page frame
subsystems.purpose: Loads a map into the browser and holds the tabs and the trail. Keeps the address in step with the screen.

subsystems.name: Diagrams and cards
subsystems.purpose: Draws the boxes, answers a click, explains the selected thing, and shows the code behind it.

subsystems.name: View pages
subsystems.purpose: The screens themselves: what the product does, what it stores, what it decides, and what a change touched.

subsystems.name: Method quality
subsystems.purpose: Answers the two questions a person changing the instructions has. Did the maps get worse, and what did that run reveal?

subsystems.name: Map scoring
subsystems.purpose: Measures one map and compares it against an accepted one. Also tests whether the challengers catch a planted falsehood.

subsystems.name: Build review
subsystems.purpose: Reads what a build actually did and what it cost, and refuses to review a run that has not finished.

subsystems.name: Eval upkeep
subsystems.purpose: Files an old map out of the way, and bundles a map with the chat that made it. Keeps the numbers written in the code honest.

components.name: Map model
components.purpose: Defines every kind of thing a map can hold. Reads a map file back and refuses one whose shape is wrong.

components.name: Shared map grammar
components.purpose: Holds the shared words and formats every other part of the map reads.

components.name: Map schema document
components.purpose: Writes a machine-readable description of the map file, for editors and other tools to read.

components.name: Map assembly
components.purpose: Merges the pieces each build agent returned into one map. Refuses two pieces that name the same thing twice.

components.name: Fragment self-check
components.purpose: Checks one agent's piece of the map before it is handed in. The agent that made a mistake is the one that fixes it.

components.name: Shape checks
components.purpose: Checks that every name in the map points at something real. Also checks that each code link is well formed and really exists.

components.name: Story checks
components.purpose: Checks the use cases, their flows and the happy path against each other. Reports the parts of the code no story covers.

components.name: Rule checks
components.purpose: Checks that each business rule names real code lines. Also writes down which files the map says guard access.

components.name: Wiring checks
components.purpose: Checks how the product connects: its interfaces, its ways in, the services it calls and the processes it runs in.

components.name: Data checks
components.purpose: Checks the saved records, their stores, who owns each data area, and how much of the map was verified.

components.name: Eval command line
components.purpose: Routes each typed eval sub-command to the checker that answers it. Loads that checker only when it is asked for.
components.depends_on: Every other checker in this tool, each opened at the moment its sub-command is typed.

components.name: Map profile
components.purpose: Reduces one built map to the numbers two builds can be compared on. Two maps of one project never share wording, so counts are what survives.
components.depends_on: The main tool's own map reader and its two checkers, so a map is never measured through a second reading of it.

components.name: Baseline comparison
components.purpose: Judges a fresh map against the accepted one. Returns one word: as good, drifted, or worse.
components.depends_on: The numbers a map profile produces, and the judged scores, when both sides carry them.

components.name: Judge report
components.purpose: Folds many skeptics' verdicts and many judges' marks into one quality report. Never talks to a model itself, so the arithmetic can be tested alone.
components.depends_on: The main tool's list of risky statements, which it samples rather than re-derives.

components.name: Eval run
components.purpose: Runs one scoring pass end to end and files everything it produced. Can then promote that run to be the accepted baseline.
components.depends_on: The map profile, the baseline comparison and the judge report, plus the main tool's renderer for the archived views.

components.name: Lost arrows
components.purpose: Finds the relations a rebuild dropped. Re-reads each dropped relation's recorded line to say whether the code still does it.
components.depends_on: The code history, to refuse the check when the two maps describe different code.

components.name: Rebuild archive
components.purpose: Moves a project's current map aside so the next build starts from nothing. Moves, never deletes: the old map is what the new one is compared against.
components.depends_on: Nothing but the file system under the mapped project.

components.name: Transcript reader
components.purpose: Turns a build's raw chat log into one record per model answer. The log stores one answer as many rows, so counting rows gets every later number wrong.
components.depends_on: The coding agent's own chat logs on disk.

components.name: Build cost
components.purpose: Reports what one build spent in time and tokens. Divides both by how much map the build produced. Two builds of different sizes then read side by side.
components.depends_on: The transcript reader, for the lead's log and every helper's log beside it.

components.name: Process scorecard
components.purpose: Scores whether the build agent behaved as the method says, one checked rule at a time. Reports numbers, never a pass or a fail.
components.depends_on: The transcript reader for what the agent did, the build cost report for how long each helper really ran, and the finished map for the rules whose subject is the map.

components.name: Retro precheck
components.purpose: Refuses a retrospective while the build it would read is still running. A build stamps who made it near the end, so mid-run the stamp still names the previous build.
components.depends_on: The mapped project's map folder, and the coding agent's chat logs for other live sessions.

components.name: Ledger check
components.purpose: Asks the code history whether a retrospective's finished items really shipped. An item still marked open, whose named change is already merged, gets proposed again for nothing.
components.depends_on: The code history of the clone holding the changes a ledger row names.

components.name: Live number ledger
components.purpose: Re-measures the counts the tools state about a map that keeps changing. Each sentence is written once in the code and once here. Nothing then has to guess which sum produced the number.
components.depends_on: The main tool's own measuring functions, called rather than copied, plus the live maps they read.

components.name: Skeptic recall test
components.purpose: Plants claims that are false by construction and keeps the answer key. Counts how many of them the skeptics caught, which is a number that means something on its own.
components.depends_on: The source tree, so a moved line lands somewhere real instead of past the end of the file.

components.name: Code survey
components.purpose: Measures how big a project's code is before the map is drawn.

components.name: Ignore list
components.purpose: Lets a project declare which of its own code the map must leave out.

components.name: Assignment rules
components.purpose: Records where every mapped thing belongs, so a rebuild keeps the decision.

components.name: Diagram balance
components.purpose: Reports how crowded each screen of the map is.

components.name: Change impact
components.purpose: Works out which parts of the map a code change touches.

components.name: Map and transcript backup
components.purpose: Bundles a finished map with the conversation that produced it.

components.name: Live reload supervisor
components.purpose: Restarts the map server when someone editing the viewer changes its code.

components.name: Product description instructions
components.purpose: Tells the mapping agent to describe the product before reading code. It orders the goal, the shared words, the people and their goals. The one successful run through those goals comes last.

components.name: Code inventory instructions
components.purpose: Says how to list what the product is made of, area by area. Every box gets a plain sentence, a code link and a confidence label. Outside services and the ways in are listed the same way.

components.name: Outside edge instructions
components.purpose: Says how to name every place the product meets the outside world. Each place gets one word for what it is, and a side saying whose design it is. It also says how a story crosses one, in both directions.

components.name: Data and step instructions
components.purpose: Says how to write the records the product keeps and the steps of each goal. A step names who acts, on what, and which way the data moves. Machinery shared by several goals is written once and referenced.

components.name: Operations and decision instructions
components.purpose: Says how to record what runs, what is watched, what is configured and what the product decides. A decision is only worth recording when a product person could have chosen otherwise. Test coverage is measured against the map, never against line counts.

components.name: Cross-cutting build instructions
components.purpose: Holds the rules that apply to every part of a build. It says how to write text a reader meets alone, with no page around it. It also sets the order of work, the tools to reach for, and how big one box may be.

components.name: Fan-out phase instructions
components.purpose: Plans the parallel work of a build in three phases. Many agents gather the pieces, one agent merges them, then many agents trace the goals. It says how to size each slice, brief it and wait for the batch.

components.name: Verification phase instructions
components.purpose: Plans what happens once every goal has been traced. Fresh agents try to disprove each claim the map makes, against the code. Two more passes write what the product decides and measure what the tests cover.

components.name: Closing sequence instructions
components.purpose: Runs the closing steps that turn a finished map into a committed one. Corrections land, the record of what was checked is written, then the gates run. It ends by telling the reader where to open the map.

components.name: Map model spec
components.purpose: States every field a map may hold and the exact shape of each. Names, code links and closed word lists are all fixed here. It also says how each part of the map is drawn on screen.

components.name: Mode dispatch instructions
components.purpose: Decides which job to do when someone calls coyomap on a project. Build a first map, report a code change, or fold a report in. It briefs the person on what will be read before anything starts.

components.name: Change impact instructions
components.purpose: Says how to report what a code change does to an existing map. The report carries the exact new text for every box it touches. Folding the report in is then mechanical, with no fresh reading of code.

components.name: Fan-out worker contracts
components.purpose: Holds the briefs handed word for word to the agents a build fans out to. One brief per job, from gathering the pieces to disproving the finished claims. The two briefs whose agents write map prose also carry the shared writing rules.

components.name: Method regression checks
components.purpose: Holds one written promise per change to the method or the tools. Each file says what the next build should do differently, and what a backfire would look like. A review of a finished build runs every check the change range added.

components.name: Build skill pointer
components.purpose: Points a coding agent at this repository so the map commands work. Kept deliberately thin, because a copy is installed into the agent and goes stale. It names the clone path and the one document to read.

components.name: Map quality eval instructions
components.purpose: Says how to score two maps of the same code and tell which one is better. A map is scored on counts, well-formedness, coverage and a model's judgement. Both maps must describe the same code, or the comparison means nothing.

components.name: Build retrospective instructions
components.purpose: Says how to review one finished build from its map and its chat. The review reports what the run revealed about the tools and the method. It changes nothing, and a standing backlog carries every proposal forward.

components.name: Public documentation
components.purpose: Explains to a newcomer what coyomap is, why it exists and how to install it. A longer page walks through how a map gets built, phase by phase. Both are read on the web by a person, never by a mapping agent.

components.name: Contributor guide
components.purpose: Says how to work on coyomap itself, for a person and for an agent alike. It names what each folder is for and which tests a given change needs. It also holds the design philosophy and the words this project uses.

components.name: Method rationale record
components.purpose: Keeps the story of the build that made each method rule necessary. Storing those stories here keeps them out of the text every build agent reads. A test checks that each entry still quotes a rule that exists.

components.name: Command line
components.purpose: Routes each typed coyomap command to the tool that runs it. The same layer decides how much of a long finding list a reader sees.

components.name: Map checks
components.purpose: Reads a finished map and reports where it contradicts itself. The same family flags a code link pointing at a line that cannot act.

components.name: Grounding record
components.purpose: Turns the skeptics' verdict files into the map's honesty record. The four counts a gate blocks on are derived, never hand-tallied.

components.name: Map editor
components.purpose: Applies one mechanical correction to a stored map in place. An edit matching no row, or more than one, is refused rather than guessed.

components.name: Map reader
components.purpose: Reads a map and never changes it. Three answers: one element's stored record, what two maps differ on, and the evidence behind a claim.

components.name: Build closer
components.purpose: Runs a build's closing steps in order and stops at the first failure. The last step writes one pre-commit verdict to a file.

components.name: Build briefing
components.purpose: Says which files a build will read and which commit its map will name. A second command prints the exact brief each helper agent is sent.

components.name: Build log
components.purpose: Records which session built a map, and when. Beside that it records how long each slice of the build took.

components.name: Map rendering
components.purpose: Turns a stored map into the readable file kept beside the code. Also builds the boxes and arrows the browser draws.

components.name: Feature facts
components.purpose: Works out what each feature owns: its people, its decisions, its records and the doors reaching it.

components.name: Diagram builder
components.purpose: Draws every diagram, timeline and flow of one map, ready for the browser page to show.

components.name: Map server
components.purpose: Serves every map on this machine at a local web address. Reads a project's own code from its version history.

components.name: File browser
components.purpose: Lists a project's folders and files, marking each one by how far the map covers it.

components.name: Remembered projects
components.purpose: Keeps the list of project folders a person has opened, so each map is one click away next time.

components.name: Map loader
components.purpose: Loads the whole map from the server when the page opens, before any screen is drawn. Glossary words in the text then become definitions you can read in place.

components.name: Element cards
components.purpose: Draws one card for anything on the map: its name, a tag saying its type, one sentence. Clicking a card opens that thing.

components.name: Diagram canvas
components.purpose: Draws a view's picture from the drawing the map recorded. Selecting a box lights it and everything it touches, and dims the rest.

components.name: Diagram clicks
components.purpose: Decides what a click does on each drawn box and arrow, view by view. Holding a key drills into a box instead of selecting it.

components.name: Info pane
components.purpose: Shows what you selected: a card floating over the picture, or a drawer along the bottom. What the pane holds changes with the kind of thing selected.

components.name: Trail and screen address
components.purpose: Keeps the tabs, the trail and the browser address in step with the screen on show. Copying that address gives someone else the same screen.

components.name: Product pages
components.purpose: Draws the pages that say what the product is for and what it does. Covers the overview, the features, the happy path, actor pages and the glossary.

components.name: Storage, tests and system pages
components.purpose: Draws the tables for where data is kept, how far the tests reach, and the operational lists.

components.name: Rules and interfaces pages
components.purpose: Draws the decisions the product makes and the places it meets the outside world. Each rule and each interface has a page of its own.

components.name: Source column
components.purpose: Shows the mapped project's files, and the source of the one you open, at the map's commit. Selecting a box on a picture opens its file here.

components.name: Viewer shell
components.purpose: Holds the page frame: the title bar, the tab rows, the panes and the settings dialog. Also wires the keyboard and the first-run guide.

components.name: Map search
components.purpose: Finds anything in the map by name as you type: elements, files, folders, glossary words. Picking a result opens it where it lives.

components.name: Impact explorer
components.purpose: Projects a code change onto the map and marks what that change touches, plus what ripples out from it. Hidden from the title bar for now.

components.name: Viewer styles
components.purpose: Holds every colour, size and layout rule the viewer page draws itself with. One stylesheet covers every view.

deps.name: Git
deps.used_for: Lists a project's files, and reads any file exactly as it stood at the map's pinned commit.

evidence.why: Asks git for the tracked and untracked files, so ignored output never enters the map.
Reads a file's contents at the map's commit, so the code viewer shows the mapped version.
Reads the commit a map is pinned to when a build is stamped.
Checks whether a recorded commit is an ancestor of the current one.

deps.name: Local file system
deps.used_for: Holds every project's map folder, the tool's own environment, and the remembered list of projects.

evidence.why: Writes the finished map beside the project's code.
Saves the list of projects the server offers on its landing page.

deps.name: Web browser
deps.used_for: Opens and draws the map viewer page for a person on this machine.

evidence.why: Opens the server's landing page in the person's browser when asked to.
The start target launches the server and opens the page.

deps.not_an_interface: The browser is the client a person reaches the viewer through, not a far side of its own.

deps.name: Code editor
deps.used_for: Receives a file and a line from the map, so a person opens that exact spot in their editor.

evidence.why: Lists the editors the viewer can hand a file to, each with its own address form.
Hands the chosen editor the file and line, which the operating system opens.

deps.name: GitHub
deps.used_for: Shows a mapped file on the web, pinned to the commit the map was built at.

evidence.why: Builds the web address of a mapped file at the map's commit.
Opens that address in a new tab when no editor is chosen.
Bug and idea reports, and private security reports, are filed on the code host.

deps.name: Coding agent
deps.used_for: Runs the installed skill that drives a map build, and names the conversation a build is stamped with.

evidence.why: Copies the skill into each agent's skills folder with this clone's path filled in.
Reads the conversation identifier the agent publishes, so a map records which chat produced it.
Reads the same conversation identifier before a build review is allowed to start.

deps.name: jsDelivr
deps.used_for: Serves the two drawing libraries the viewer page loads in the browser.

evidence.why: The page loads the diagram library from this host, pinned to a version and a checksum.

deps.not_an_interface: Its scripts are fetched into the viewer page and become part of it, so no data crosses a surface.

deps.name: Mermaid
deps.used_for: Draws every diagram on the viewer page from the text the tool generates.

evidence.why: Loaded as one self-contained bundle so the checksum covers the whole library.
Generates the diagram text this library turns into a picture.

deps.not_an_interface: A library the viewer page loads and becomes part of.

deps.name: svg-pan-zoom
deps.used_for: Lets a person pan and zoom a drawn diagram in the viewer.

evidence.why: Loaded from the delivery network, pinned to a version and a checksum.

deps.not_an_interface: A library the viewer page loads and becomes part of.

deps.name: tree-sitter
deps.used_for: Reads symbols and imports out of source files in many languages during the first pass.

evidence.why: Builds a parser for one language, and gives up quietly when the library is absent.
Declared as an optional extra, so the core of the tool stays free of outside packages.

deps.not_an_interface: A library the code survey imports and becomes part of.

deps.name: tree-sitter language pack
deps.used_for: Supplies the per-language grammars the source parser needs.

evidence.why: Tries to load the pack, and records why it failed when it is missing.
Fetches one language's grammar for the parser.

deps.not_an_interface: A library the code survey imports and becomes part of.

deps.name: pytest
deps.used_for: Runs the whole test suite, which is the first half of the checks a change must pass.

evidence.why: The checks target runs the suite with no folder named, so no tests are silently skipped.
Declares the two test folders that a bare run collects.

deps.not_an_interface: A library the checks run under and become part of.

deps.name: pyright
deps.used_for: Checks the tool's Python types, which is the second half of the checks a change must pass.

evidence.why: The checks target runs the type checker after the tests, so one run reports everything.
Tells the type checker where the two source folders live.

steps.phrase: ask the coding agent for a map of this project
point the agent at the coyomap clone and the one document to read
read the method end to end and plan the build as waves of helper agents
size each helper's slice from a survey of the project's code
count the files, lines and symbols of the project's own code
fill each helper's brief from the shared contract
steps.note: a slot left empty is refused, so no helper is briefed on the wrong thing

steps.phrase: make each helper self-check its own piece before handing it in
turn the path rules into one assignment for every mapped thing
record where every mapped thing belongs before the merge
merge every returned piece into one map
gather every piece the helpers wrote, and name the ones that failed
write the merged map into the project's map folder
hand the finished map to fresh agents that try to disprove it
hand the corrected map to the closing sequence
run the closing steps in order and stop at the first failure
turn the skeptics' votes into the map's honesty record
write how much of the map was challenged and how the votes fell
stamp which session built the map, and when
name the finished map's files and the address that opens it
hand back the finished map and the checks it passed

flows.title: See what a code change did to the map

steps.phrase: ask what the newer code did to the map
point the coding agent at the method in the coyomap clone
read the change-impact instructions and follow them
read the commit the map is pinned to
diff the pinned commit against the working tree, untracked files included
read the changed code and classify each change as modified, added or deleted
follow the map's arrows out to every element the change reaches
write the report, carrying the exact new text of every element it touches
leave the report on disk beside the map
steps.note: uncommitted until the person accepts it

steps.phrase: name every part of the map the change touched, and what each should now say

flows.title: Fold a change report into the baseline

steps.phrase: agree the report is right and ask to fold it into the map
point the coding agent at the method in the coyomap clone
read the accept steps and follow them
read back the new text the report already carries for every element it touches
steps.note: accept re-reads no code and infers nothing

steps.phrase: apply each was-to-now block to the stored map
write the corrected rows back into the stored map
stamp this accept session and re-pin the map to the code commit
read the commit the code now stands at
ask whether to commit the code first, or pin the map as dirty
steps.note: only when the code is uncommitted

steps.phrase: put the two choices in front of the person
commit the code, then say to go on
carry the answer back to the accept steps
write the build stamp beside the map
rebuild the code survey at the new pin
steps.note: only when the map already has one

steps.phrase: list the project's tracked and untracked files
write the code survey beside the map
commit the map, its readable view, the code survey and the report together
hand back the address that opens this project's map
give the person the address of the re-pinned map
write one ignore pattern per line beside the map
steps.note: The file is committed with the code. A .gitignore cannot say 'tracked, yet not part of what the map describes'.

steps.phrase: hand over the pattern lines in the order they were written
steps.note: The last rule that matches a path is the one that decides it. So a `!` line carves an exception out of a broad ignore. A line whose `#` sits mid-line is one literal pattern, and is reported as unusable.

steps.phrase: ask for the briefing that says what will be read
carry the request to describe the tree, and nothing else
walk the project's files, the same walk the survey and the checks use
ask which rule decides each file the walk found
record which files stayed and how many each rule took out
steps.note: The tally is kept on the walk, not on the parsed file. So one project's counts can never be reported for another.

steps.phrase: ask what each pattern took out, for the briefing
print the file count and every pattern beside what it took out
show the narrowed tree before any code is read
write the per-pattern counts into the code survey beside the map
ask for the map's own checks to run
carry the check request, whether the cheap pass or the full one
walk the tree again instead of trusting the code survey
steps.note: Each coverage check re-measures the repo on its own. The ignore file is the one input both sides read, so it is always disclosed.

steps.phrase: ask what each pattern decided on that second walk
name every pattern that decided nothing on this tree
steps.note: A pattern that took nothing out is a typo, or a tree that moved. Left unsaid it reads as coverage the author never got.

steps.phrase: show what the map was told to leave out, on every check run
ask in plain language to move, split or rename part of the map
point the agent at the clone and at the one document that decides the mode
run the map commands the method names
carry the request to read one element's stored record
read the stored record of the element the person named
carry the request for a proposed split of one crowded screen
print a proposed grouping for a screen that holds too many boxes
show the split as a starting point, never as ready to apply
carry one addressed row rewrite, refusing an address that matches none or many
merge the harvest pieces first, so an edit that would mint or retire an id is refused
steps.note: Rows are merged by their own text. Rewriting that text can split one row in two, or collapse two into one.

tests_note: The table was built by reading the two test suites, never by running them. No coverage numbers were measured.

tests.label: Refusing to overwrite coyomap's own map
tests.gap: Nothing exercises the refusal that protects the coyomap clone's own map. A build started in the wrong folder could overwrite it.

tests.label: Refusing to read coyomap's own map by mistake

tests.why: Every map reader among the build commands passes through the refusal.
The refusal prints one plain line, never a crash dump.
Someone mapping coyomap itself can still switch the refusal off.

tests.gap: Three commands are driven for real. The rest are covered only by a scan of the source text.

tests.label: Turning away a request that names another machine

tests.why: The name check accepts this machine and refuses every other name.

tests.gap: No test sends a real request carrying a foreign name. A wiring slip in the map server would go unnoticed.

tests.label: Guard on requests that change the project list
tests.gap: No test ever sends a change request to the map server. A web page you visit could edit your project list.

tests.label: Adding, dropping and reordering remembered projects

tests.why: The remembered project list adds, removes, de-duplicates and survives a restart.
A new order for the remembered projects is saved and read back.

tests.gap: The three network addresses that drive those changes are never called. Only the storage under them is tested.

tests.label: Listing any folder on this machine

tests.why: Folder listing marks each folder that already holds a map.

tests.gap: The address the browser calls is never exercised. Nothing checks the answer for a folder that does not exist.

tests.label: Health answer naming the pinned commit
tests.gap: No test asks the map server whether it is answering. A break there shows only as a page that never loads.

tests.label: Serving one file's text at the pinned commit

tests.why: One file's text is served at the pinned commit and at another commit.
Ignored files, the version-control folder and paths that climb out are refused.
A path that climbs above the project folder is rejected.

tests.gap: No test feeds a file big enough to hit the size limit. A limit that stopped working shows only as a stalled page.

tests.label: Closing sequence that ships a build

tests.why: The closing sequence lists its steps in the order the method sets.
A failing step stops the run and names the steps left undone.

tests.gap: Every step runs against a stand-in, never the real command. A change inside one command can still break the sequence.

tests.label: One pre-commit verdict over every check

tests.why: A clean map succeeds and writes both of its reports.
A blocking problem fails the run and is recorded as blocking.
A check that never ran can never be reported as clean.
A faked count of challenged claims is caught by recomputing it.

tests.gap: The suite feeds hand-built maps. No test runs the verdict over a map a real build just produced.

tests.label: Honesty record of what the doubters challenged

tests.why: Verdict files are checked for shape, folded into votes and written back.
Each element gets the review outcome the votes actually support.

tests.gap: Nothing checks the record against a full real build's verdict files.

tests.label: Editing map rows in one all-or-nothing write

tests.why: Two corrections landing on one row are both refused, so nothing half-lands.
A conflicting duplicate is reported and no change is written.
An edit that would split a merged row is refused.

tests.gap: No test interrupts a write midway. A crash during the write is not covered.

tests.label: Merging the build agents' fragments into one map

tests.why: Merging the stored fragments gives the same bytes every time.
Every stored fragment passes the self-check a build agent runs.
Conflicts, duplicates and missing pieces across fragments are resolved or reported.
A fragment with invented ids or bad wording is refused before merging.

tests.gap: The stored fragment set is one project's. A shape only another project produces would not be met.

tests.label: Checks a map must pass to be well formed

tests.why: Four hundred cases cover shape, story, rule, wiring and data checks.
Places where a map contradicts itself are found and reported.
Deliberately broken maps are caught rather than passed.

tests.gap: A check that is too loose still passes its own test. Only the trap maps push back on that.

tests.label: Survey of the code a build starts from

tests.why: The survey walks the files, names the symbols and counts the sizes.
Directory expectations and size bands come out at the right grain.
Only files version control tracks are walked.

tests.gap: The survey reads fifteen languages. Tests feed only Python and JavaScript, so thirteen parsers are unproven.

tests.label: Leaving named code off the map

tests.why: Ignored paths drop out of the survey, the file tree and the counts.

tests.gap: No test runs a whole build with an ignore list and checks the printed counts.

tests.label: Assigning code to groups and balancing the diagrams

tests.why: Path rules expand into an explicit assignment for every file.
Diagrams holding too many boxes are named with a suggested split.

tests.gap: Balance is judged on small hand-built maps. Nothing checks the advice on a map the size of a real project.

tests.label: Map data shape, shared words and schema

tests.why: Every part of a map loads, saves and round-trips without loss.
The fixed word lists stay closed and agree with the model.
The published schema still matches the data shape it describes.
Notes headings are read into the sections a map stores.

tests.gap: The schema check compares shapes. Nothing validates a real map file against the schema itself.

tests.label: Briefing that tells a build what to read

tests.why: The list of files a build will read is produced before it starts.
Each helper agent's brief is printed complete and with the right ids.

tests.gap: No test proves a brief a helper agent receives is one it can actually follow.

tests.label: Build log of sessions and slice timings

tests.why: The session that built a map is stamped and listed back.
What each build slice took is recorded and sorted longest first.

tests.gap: Nothing checks the log after a real build. Only hand-written entries are read back.

tests.label: Report of what a code change did to the map

tests.why: A change between two commits is matched to the map parts it touches.
A hit on one box spreads to the boxes and steps that depend on it.
The report also comes back correctly over the network.

tests.gap: Repositories in the tests are tiny. A change touching hundreds of files is never tried.

tests.label: Every command surviving a realistic map

tests.why: A new command cannot ship without joining the sweep that runs it.
Every command runs against a real map without crashing.
Every command refuses an option it does not know.
No command hangs waiting for a person to type.

tests.gap: The map server is the one command left out, because starting it blocks. Its behaviour is checked elsewhere.

tests.label: Restarting the map server when the viewer changes
tests.gap: Nothing tests the watcher that restarts the map server. A silent failure leaves developers looking at stale screens.

tests.label: Archiving a map with the conversation that built it
tests.gap: Nothing tests the backup that moves a map and its chat aside. A bug there loses work with no warning.

tests.label: File tree marked by how far the map covers it

tests.why: Folders and files come back marked by how much of the map reaches them.

tests.gap: The tree is built from small fixtures. A repository with deep nesting is not tried.

tests.label: Turning a map into diagrams and cards

Boxes land in the right groups and lanes on every picture.
Processes, queues and the arrows between them are drawn correctly.
Each feature's facts are gathered from the flows that reach it.

tests.gap: The pictures are checked as data, not as drawings. A layout that overlaps still passes.

tests.label: Screen addresses and the trail back

tests.why: A reload comes back to the exact screen you were on.

grounding.note:
Twenty-five fresh-context skeptics challenged every claim in the pinned worklist, in two waves, with the behavioural theme turned on. This pass has 790 verdict rows over 728 distinct claims, 54 of them repeat rows from re-voting, and 25 distinct skeptic labels. Confirmed 719, refuted 9, unverifiable 0, tied 0. Ten cheap readers judged the map's 371 reader-facing sentences separately; 19 were flagged and 4 were rewritten, the rest being one reader's taste rather than a defect.

THE THREE-VOTER RECORD BROKE. The whole access theme got three independent voters. Across 27 multi-voted claims they disagreed on 2 verdicts and on 4 evidence anchors. Four earlier builds recorded no verdict disagreement at all, so that run of unanimity ends here, on the first build under the revised skeptic brief. The dissenter was right: it followed every call site of the version-name guard and ran it, and showed that no web address reaches the two lines the map cited, while the other two voters confirmed those lines without following the callers. This is the experiment the retro backlog parked as its open question 6, and the answer is that the vote does buy something.

ELEVEN REFUTATIONS WERE RAISED AND ALL ELEVEN WENT TO AN INDEPENDENT CLOSER, denied the map and denied this build's reasoning. It upheld ten and could not settle the eleventh, because that claim is a derived fact and its brief carried only the surface's own row, not the story steps behind it. I settled that one myself by reading the build file: installing the developer skills is a separate opt-in target whose own comment says it is never part of setting the tool up, so the install story wrongly stood the map owner at the developer surface. I removed those six steps. That is my read, not the closer's.

TWENTY CLAIMS WERE SUPERSEDED AND ELEVEN OF THEM HAD BEEN CONFIRMED — each a settled verdict this build overrode. Two are the access sites at the version-name guard, confirmed 2 to 1 and dropped anyway on the closer's uphold, with the line the closer showed does guard a web address added in their place. The other nine are sentences and steps I rewrote from advice the skeptics gave inside a confirming verdict, which is the outcome that otherwise disappears because the verdict itself reads clean.

WHAT WAS NOT RE-CHALLENGED: 11 claims were added since the pin, so no skeptic has read them. Each is a correction to a sentence or to an anchor, grounded in a line the closer or a skeptic read and quoted, and none of them adds a new relationship to the map.

ONE MEASUREMENT ON THE EVIDENCE ITSELF. The verdict lint reports 70 rows across 16 files where the file a skeptic cites appears in its own transcript only as printed text, never as a file it opened. That is not proof of anything, since a range read through a shell command looks identical, but it is the shape a fabricating pass would have, and it is recorded here rather than left unsaid.

Two confirmed claims had drifted anchors; both were corrected through the reconcile file, so the fix survives a rebuild.

Reports the self-started ways in that no story reaches, in the same grouped shape.

sites.why: refuses a reason filed under a heading no check ever reads

rules.statement: Only files git accounts for are analysed, so ignored and generated trees stay out of the map.

rules.statement: A project's own exclusion patterns are named on every run, each beside the number of files it removed.

rules.statement: A build never opens the map it is replacing, so the new map cannot quietly copy the old one.

extras.heading: Balance exceptions
extras.body:
granularity: 79 boxes against a code-derived 26. Most of the gap is prose. This product keeps about 11,700 lines of its logic in instruction files, and the expectation counts code only. The rest is two single files. A 6,700-line checker and a 3,150-line instruction document were each cut into their named parts, rather than left as one box nobody can point inside.
runs-in/entry-hosts: The one unplaced thread is the live-reload watcher a contributor starts by hand. It is not a delivered process, so no deployment unit hosts it.
UC1: Installing is all crossings. Every action of it is declared in the build file, which no component owns, so there is no honest step of the product's own machinery in between.
SF2: The name was prescribed by the lead as a shared id that three other stories reference by name. Renaming it would break those references. It is one goal, the closing run of the gates.
UC2: Building a map is genuinely the longest story this product tells, and it already hands two runs of shared machinery to their own sub-flows. Compressing it further would hide the phases a reader most wants to see.
security-granularity: family — one rule per surface family, not one per address and condition. This product has no accounts and no roles, so its eight access rules are guards on what a build may open and what the local server hands back.

extras.heading: Bucket vocabulary
extras.body:
Source and history: The product reads a project's own files and past versions. No seed names that purpose, and folding it into the catch-all would hide the one outside thing every build depends on.
Code navigation: Two outside things exist only so a reader can open a mapped line somewhere else. That is a purpose, not a catch-all.
Source parsing: Reading names out of source in many languages. The library seeds name no parsing purpose at all.
Testing & type checking: The two gates a change must pass. No seed covers them, and calling them tooling would say nothing.
Build & packaging: Installing the product from its own repo. No seed covers packaging.

extras.heading: Entry-point coverage
extras.body:
cli: complete — walked the whole command table in the dispatcher, and each command's own argument parser, for both command lines.
http-route: complete — walked every branch of the map server's request handler.
ui-route: complete — walked the tab buttons in the page shell and every drill address the page dispatches.
agent-tools: complete — the three installed skill files, one per slash command.
startup-hook: complete — the map server's own boot work.
poller: complete — the two repeat loops found by reading the server and the live-reload supervisor.
cli naming: Nine of the eleven stories arrive through a slash command or a screen, and the commands they run are steps inside those stories. Only the two a person types directly are named as a front door.
http-route naming: Every web address here is fetched by the viewer page after the reader has already arrived. The page is the door, and the stories name that.

extras.heading: Happy Path coverage
extras.body:
R3: The method author is the person who changes coyomap itself. Their work acts on maps that already exist, so it sits beside the product's story rather than inside it.
CAP5: Improving the method is the developer's own loop. A person mapping their project never runs it, so the happy path deliberately does not reach it.

extras.heading: Interface exceptions
extras.body:
I8: The files read are the mapped project's own, which this product never wrote. The call site cannot show that, because it opens a path like any other.
I9: An address is built and handed over, and nothing comes back. No call site can show what crosses when only the person does.
I10: Same shape as the editor. A link is built and handed to the reader, so the crossing happens in their browser, not at our line.
I11: The chat files are written by the coding agent, not by this product. A read of a path cannot show whose file it is.
UC1/doors: Each door is anchored where the install acts, in the build file. The command line has no way in of its own for a build target, so no way in carries the line.

extras.heading: Unclaimed surfaces
extras.body:
C50: Bundling a map with the conversation that made it is the developer's own upkeep. No story a person mapping their project would tell reaches it.
C51: The watcher restarts the map server when a contributor edits the viewer. It serves nobody outside the product, so no actor can claim it.

extras.heading: Coverage exceptions
extras.body: conftest.py: The one loose file at the repo root wires the test run. This map deliberately leaves the test suites out of its boxes and answers them on the Tests screen instead.

extras.heading: Data owner exceptions
extras.body: SD10, SD11, SD12, SD13, SD14: Every record in these areas is kept inside the map file, which has its own area. The build's story touches the map file itself, so the evidence sits one level up rather than on each record.

extras.heading: Sweep debt
extras.body:
tools/coyomap/viewer/viewer.js:14928: The step hands a link to the reader. The decision behind it is which version of the code that link points at, and a rule already claims that.
skill/coyomap/SKILL.md:27: The step points the agent at one document. It carries no choice: the pointer is the same on every build.
eval/retro/method.md:62: This IS a decision, and no block covers it. The decision grouping has no area for reviewing a finished build, so the sweep is honestly in debt here.

extras.heading: Audit exceptions
extras.body: read-never-created HP4: The drawn boxes are built fresh from the map each time a screen opens. Nothing stores them, so no step can create them.

extras.heading: Access baseline exceptions
extras.body: method/dispatch.md: I read both lines. They tell a build not to reopen the map it is replacing, and not to pull a deleted one back out of version control. That protects the map's independence, not permission, so it is a decision this map keeps without calling it access control.
